messages.subject_clean: how to stop the simulation when a given condition is met
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I've got so excited after working with some of simmer tutorials that I decided to use it right away in my modeling and simulation course.
Of course, I should have waited a bit longer to learn it better!. Now I am in the middle of the course learning as it goes with no much time to
tinker with the library.

I am trying to solve what I thought was a fairly easy exercise in simmer. The problem is as follow:

# A superhighway connects one large metropolitan area to another. A vehicle leaves
# the first city every 20 ± 15 seconds. Twenty percent of the vehicles have l passenger,
# 30% of the vehicles have 2 passengers, 10% have 3 passengers, and 10% have 4 passengers.
# The remaining 30% of the vehicles are buses, which cany 40 people.
# It takes 60 ± 10 minutes for a vehicle to travel between the two metropolitan areas.
# How long does it take for 5000 people to arrive in the second city?

This comes from the book of Banks, Carson, et al.

I am having problems trying to stop the simulation as specified. It just keeps running until the specified time
ends. Could somebody please help me to figure out what I am doing wrong?
Although variable names and log messages are in Spanish, I think it is easy to understand the code anyway.

I use 500 instead of 5000 for testing. Here is the code:

set.seed(1269)
autopista <- simmer()

iniciar <- trajectory() %>%
  set_global(keys="total",values=0)

automovil <-
  trajectory("Trayectoria de los vehiculos") %>%
  set_attribute(keys="tipo", value=function(){sample(1:5,1,prob=c(0.2,0.3,0.1,0.1,0.3))}) %>%
  log_(function() {paste("Salio tipo: ", get_attribute(autopista,"tipo"))}) %>%
  timeout(function() {runif(1, 50,70)}) %>%
  set_global(keys="total",function(){ get_attribute(autopista,"total",global=TRUE) + ifelse(get_attribute(autopista,"tipo") <= 4,
                                                  get_attribute(autopista,"tipo"),
                                                  40)})  %>%
  log_(function() {paste("Van: ", get_attribute(autopista,"total",global=TRUE))}) %>%
  log_(function() {paste("LLego: ", now(autopista))}) %>%
  branch(function() {ifelse(get_global(autopista,"total") >= 500,1,2)},continue=c(T,T),
         trajectory() %>%
           seize("branch1", 1) %>%
           deactivate("vehiculo") %>%
           release("branch1"),
         trajectory() %>%
           seize("branch2", 1) %>%
           activate("vehiculo")%>%
           release("branch2"))

autopista <-
  simmer("autopista") %>%
  add_generator("iniciar",iniciar,at(0)) %>%
  add_generator("vehiculo", automovil, function() {runif(1, 5, 35)},mon=2) %>%
  add_resource("branch1", Inf) %>%
  add_resource("branch2", Inf)

autopista %>% run(1000)
llegadas <- get_mon_arrivals(autopista,ongoing=TRUE,per_resource=TRUE)
atri <-get_mon_attributes(autopista)

And this is the last part of the trace. At the end of the simulation 3006 personas have arrived, but
the simulation did not stop.

430.123: vehiculo210: Van:  3002
430.123: vehiculo210: LLego:  430.122687129769
430.654: vehiculo207: Van:  3005
430.654: vehiculo207: LLego:  430.654050514568
431.553: vehiculo208: Van:  3006
431.553: vehiculo208: LLego:  431.552946756128
simmer environment: autopista | now: 431.552946756128 | next:

Thanks!

Magdiel

Currently, simmer doesn't implement any mechanism to *cleanly* stop a
simulation under a given criterion. However, R is very flexible, and

use this in our behalf. A minimal example:

library(simmer)
set.seed(42)

t <- trajectory() %>%
  set_global("counter", function() {
    counter <- get_global(env, "counter") + 1
    if (is.na <http://is.na>(counter)) counter <- 1 # initialisation
    if (counter == 500) stop("500 arrivals")
    counter
  })

env <- simmer()
env %>%
  add_generator("dummy", t, function() rexp(100, 2)) %>%
  run()
#> Error in run_(private$sim_obj, until) : Evaluation error: 500 arrivals.
now(env)
#> 276.1731

That's it. Nevertheless, I'm not a fan of this workaround. This is why
there's an alternative on the roadmap. See:

https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer/issues/100

messages.subject: Build up a finite queue without rejecting arrivals
messages.subject_clean: Build up a finite queue without rejecting arrivals
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

As I understand finite queues now, when a queue is maxed out an an arrival comes - that unit is kicked out of the simulation.

I am designing a simulation model for a paint fill line at a manufacturing plant. Each machine in the fill has a finite queue size which, if reached, causes the previous machine in the line to temporarily shut down until the queue has been emptied (instead of just kicking of the arrival), and this would occur as a chain reaction until things clear up. Does that make sense?

Is there a way to accomplish this using the reject parameter of the seize function? Or is there another way this would be done more easily?

Let me know your thoughts. Love the package.

Best,
John

> Hello,
>
> As I understand finite queues now, when a queue is maxed out an an arrival
> comes - that unit is kicked out of the simulation.

Yes, by default, it is.

> I am designing a simulation model for a paint fill line at a manufacturing
> plant. Each machine in the fill has a finite queue size which, if reached,
> causes the previous machine in the line to temporarily shut down until the
> queue has been emptied (instead of just kicking of the arrival), and this
> would occur as a chain reaction until things clear up. Does that make sense?

It does. This is a very interesting use case, and a tricky one.

> Is there a way to accomplish this using the reject parameter of the seize
> function? Or is there another way this would be done more easily?

Well, let's analyse the requisites. Despite the limited queue,
arrivals must not be dropped, so you *do* need to use the 'reject'
parameter, and the trajectory specified there must somehow stop all
the machines before that point. Stopping a machine means that the
ongoing processes must be stopped. This is achieved if a higher
priority arrival seizes the whole resource causing preemption.
Therefore, all the machines must be preemptive resources.

Summing up, an arrival following a 'reject' trajectory in a given
machine should trigger another higher priority arrival responsible for
capturing all the machines in the line until things clear up (i.e.,
the machine that caused the stop condition is released). Therefore,
after releasing a given machine, each arrival should emit a signal,
just in case the higher priority arrival was waiting to release
stopped machines.

There are other considerations. For example, some global attributes
should keep track of which machines are stopped to avoid re-capturing
them. This could happen if two (or more) different machines in
different points of the line cause a stop condition.

Also, the arrival that followed the 'reject' path should be stopped
until things clear up, and then it should rollback to try to seize the
machine again. If arrivals seize the next machine as soon as they
release the previous one, a simple 'trap/wait' (waiting for the signal
we were talking about before) should do the trick. But if some time is
required between machines, an additional resource between every pair
of consecutive machines would be needed (single capacity, infinite
queue; representing that part of the distribution line).

For sure there are finer details missing in this analysis, but I think
it's a good start. Please, keep us posted on your thoughts and your
progress.

Regards,
Iñaki

messages.body_plain:
This is a common pattern. I've heard it referred to as "interleaved resources" among other things.
The usual approach is to seize a token from the next resource prior to releasing the current one.
This ensures there is a spot available, and if not, the entity just sits still after completing its delay (processing time).
This propagates the wait backwards but only as the buffers between machines reach capacity rather than shutting them all down the moment any machine in the line reaches capacity.
So instead of the usual trio:
seize1-delay1-release1-seize2-delay2-release2...
switch to:
seize1-delay1-seize2-release1-delay2-seize3-release2...
You can use this same approach for nested work stations.

> This is a common pattern. I've heard it referred to as "interleaved
> resources" among other things.
> The usual approach is to seize a token from the next resource prior to
> releasing the current one.
> This ensures there is a spot available, and if not, the entity just sits

> This propagates the wait backwards but only as the buffers between machines
> reach capacity rather than shutting them all down the moment any machine in
> the line reaches capacity.
> So instead of the usual trio:
> seize1-delay1-release1-seize2-delay2-release2...

> seize1-delay1-seize2-release1-delay2-seize3-release2...
> You can use this same approach for nested work stations.

If there is some time required to reach the next resource after
releasing the previous one, then the interleaved pattern won't work.

Also note that there is another drawback: if the next resource is
seized but the server is busy (the arrival enters the queue), the
previous resource is not released until the arrival leaves the queue,
causing blockage. This might or might not be desired depending on the
use case.

If this is undesired, then a pattern similar to what I've posted in
the other thread [1] could be helpful. Something in the lines of

- seize A
- timeout based on some distribution
- branch, if B is not available (queue is full)
  - wait until a signal is received from an arrival releasing B
- release A
- seize B

John, I would try this pattern first if you don't require any delay
between the last two steps. If you do need some delay, then you can
use an auxiliary resource representing the distribution line from A to
B:

- seize A
- timeout based on some distribution
- branch, if AtoB is not available (queue is full)
  - wait until a signal is received from an arrival releasing AtoB
- release A
- seize AtoB
- timeout to reach B
- branch, if B is not available (queue is full)
  - wait until a signal is received from an arrival releasing B
- release AtoB
- seize B

etc. If this doesn't meet your needs, then you can try a more complex
approach as I described in my first email.

Iñaki

Check this: https://r-simmer.org/articles/simmer-03-trajectories.html#send-trap-untrap-wait

The most general pattern would be

library(simmer)
library(simmer.bricks)
library(simmer.plot)

interleaved_resources <- function(.trj, names, delays) {
  for (i in seq_along(names)) {
    .trj %>%
      seize(names[i]) %>%
      timeout(delays[i])

    if (i < length(names)) .trj %>%
      seize(paste(names[i+1], "token"), continue=TRUE,
            reject = trajectory() %>%
              wait_until(paste(names[i+1], "released")) %>%
              rollback(4)) # to seize the token

    .trj %>%
      release(names[i]) %>%
      send(paste(names[i], "released"))
  }

  .trj
}

t <- trajectory() %>%
  interleaved_resources(c("A", "B", "C"), c(1, 2, 1))
plot(t)

In your simulation, A would be the first machine, B would be a
conveyor belt from A to C, C would be the second machine, etc.

Hi all,

I've just merged this new feature into the master branch. Monitoring
has always been performed in-memory, which is convenient and fast, but
may lead to memory issues for very long simulations. Now, it is
possible to offload this to disk:

library(simmer)
to_csv <- monitor_csv()
env <- simmer(mon=to_csv)
env
#> simmer environment: anonymous | now: 0 | next:
#> { Monitor: to disk (delimited files) }
#>  { arrivals: /tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_arrivals.csv }
#>  { releases: /tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_releases.csv }
#>  { attributes: /tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_attributes.csv }
#>  { resources: /tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_resources.csv }

As you can see, data tables are saved into the R tempdir by default,
although it is possible to specify any valid location (see
"?monitor_csv()"). Functions get_mon_arrivals() and the like will work
as usual to load these files into data frames. However, if you want to
process the data in a separate workflow, then you can obtain the file
names from the monitor object:

to_csv$handlers
#>                                    arrivals
#>  "/tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_arrivals.csv"
#>                                    releases
#>   "/tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_releases.csv"
#>                                  attributes
#> "/tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_attributes.csv"
#>                                   resources
#> "/tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_resources.csv"

I'd appreciate if you can test this feature and provide your feedback
before the next release, which will be in two weeks.

Regards,

2018-04-23 16:12 GMT+02:00  <david.j...@gmail.com>:
> Is it possible to change an arrival's prioritization while in queue for a
> resource?

Enqueued arrivals are inactive by definition, and cannot perform any
action. You can set a reneging condition though, change the priority
and retry.

Consider for instance the following simulation:

t <- trajectory() %>%
  seize("res") %>%
  timeout(2) %>%
  release("res")

simmer() %>%
  add_resource("res") %>%
  add_generator("high_p", t, function() 1, priority=1) %>%
  add_generator("low_p", t, at(3)) %>%
  run(20) %>%
  get_mon_arrivals()

The low_p arrival, at 3, will never take the chance to seize the
resource, because there is always a new high_p arrival that takes the
front of the queue. But

t <- trajectory() %>%
  renege_in(
    5,
    out = trajectory() %>%
      set_prioritization(c(2, 2, FALSE)) %>%
      rollback(2) # back to "renege_in"
  ) %>%
  seize("res") %>%
  timeout(2) %>%
  release("res")

simmer() %>%
  add_resource("res") %>%
  add_generator("high_p", t, function() 1, priority=1) %>%
  add_generator("low_p", t, at(3)) %>%
  run(20) %>%
  get_mon_arrivals()

Now the low_p arrival reneges at 8, increases its priority and
retries. It has to wait another unit of time for the server to be
available, but now it is in the front of the queue and takes the
server at 9.

The "times" argument (infinite by default) defines the number of times

...

...

    discharge,
